title: Exfiltration and sensitive disclosure through output
summary: Data leaves through what the model writes: Markdown images and links that the client fetches, secrets pasted into answers, and a system prompt used as a control.
useIf: The model sees any private data and its output is rendered, forwarded or passed to tools.
avoidIf: You need to decide who may read which document. That is access control, which comes before output control.

explain.md: Output is an exit. If injected text tells the model to append a Markdown image whose URL contains private data, the client may fetch it automatically and the attacker reads the data from their server logs. EchoLeak used this shape: reference-style Markdown to avoid link redaction, auto-fetched images and an allowed Teams proxy [[r6]]. OWASP LLM05 treats model output like any untrusted input: encode it for its context and apply strict content security policies [[tr4]].

explain.title: Markdown image exfiltration
explain.alt: Injected text makes the model write an image link with data in the URL. The client fetches the image and the attacker server receives the data.
explain.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant D as Poisoned document
  participant M as Model
  participant C as Client
  participant A as Attacker server
  D->>M: Hidden instruction
  M->>C: Answer with image URL carrying data
  C->>A: Auto-fetch image
  A-->>A: Data stored in request log

explain.title: The pattern to block (illustrative)
explain.caption: The query string is the payload. The image itself is irrelevant.

explain.md: Two more disclosure paths matter. **LLM02** covers sensitive data reaching answers through retrieval, which access control prevents upstream [[tr2]]. **LLM07** says the system prompt must not be treated as a secret or a security control, and that the real risk is delegating authorization to the model or storing sensitive data in the prompt [[tr6]].

Controls, strongest first: remove the capability (do not auto-load remote images), allowlist hosts or rewrite URLs through a proxy you control, set a strict content security policy, scan output for secrets and personal data, and require approval before any outbound action. Each is deterministic except the scanner.

explain.title: Allowed proxies are exits too
explain.md: EchoLeak got data out through a proxy the policy trusted. After you allowlist a host, check what that host forwards.

whereToUse: Chat clients that render Markdown, HTML, images or link previews
Assistants that pass output to email, tickets, code or database tools
Any system prompt that contains keys, connection strings, role maps or business rules
Support bots that must not echo personal data from retrieved text

use: Private data and rendered output share a session
The prompt holds anything you would not publish
avoid: Using a prompt instruction as the only output control
Scanning output for secrets while leaving image auto-fetch enabled
Running a slow full-answer judge on a streaming, latency-bound path
flips: The client shows plain text only: drop image controls, keep sensitive-data scans
Output feeds code or SQL: apply context-specific encoding and parameterisation before anything else

pitfalls.symptom: A link redaction filter is in place, yet a linked image still carries data out
pitfalls.cause: Filters match one Markdown form and miss reference-style links
pitfalls.fix: Parse Markdown properly or render as text, then allowlist hosts

pitfalls.symptom: A leaked system prompt triggers a security incident
pitfalls.cause: Keys or authorization rules were stored in the prompt
pitfalls.fix: Keep secrets and role logic in code outside the model, and treat the prompt as public

pitfalls.cause: The scanner needs a full sentence or answer before it can decide
pitfalls.fix: Scan in small windows, and accept a short delay for sensitive tiers only

scenarios.title: Markdown rendering in an internal chat
scenarios.situation: An internal assistant sees confidential documents and its chat client renders Markdown images and links automatically. Some retrieved sources are written by external partners.
unknowns: Can the client restrict image hosts?
scenarios.question: What do you change first?

options.name: Add a prompt-injection classifier on partner documents
options.tradeoff: Probabilistic, and the exit path stays open for any bypass.

options.name: Stop auto-fetching images and rewrite links to an allowlist, with a strict content security policy
options.why: It closes the exit deterministically, whatever the model wrote.
options.tradeoff: Inline images from other hosts no longer load.

options.name: Tell the model never to output URLs
options.why: An injected instruction can override the line, and legitimate citations need links.
options.tradeoff: A useful hint inside a layered design only.

flips.if: No private data can enter the session
flips.then: The exfiltration risk falls to nuisance level and detection is enough.
Host them behind your own proxy and audit what the proxy forwards.

scenarios.takeaway: Close the output exit before improving detection.

scenarios.title: Secrets in the system prompt
scenarios.situation: A team put a database connection string and a role table in the system prompt so the model can decide what users may do. A tester extracted the prompt in minutes.
unknowns: Where is the real authorization decision made today?
scenarios.question: What is the fix?

options.name: Add a line telling the model never to reveal the prompt
options.why: OWASP says the prompt should not be considered secret, and a refusal rule is bypassable.

options.name: Rotate the credentials, remove them from the prompt, and enforce roles in code outside the model
options.why: It removes the secret and the delegated authorization, which are the real risk in LLM07.
options.tradeoff: Needs a role check in the tool or retrieval layer.

options.name: Encrypt the prompt text before sending it
options.why: The model must read the prompt, so whatever it reads it can reveal.
options.tradeoff: Encryption helps at rest and in transit, not against the model.

flips.if: The prompt holds only tone and format rules
flips.then: Leakage is low impact and needs no special control.
Scope tool credentials to the user, not the prompt.

scenarios.takeaway: Assume the system prompt is public.

scenarios.title: Personal data in support answers
scenarios.situation: A high-volume support bot retrieves tickets that contain names, phone numbers and account ids. Answers stream to users and the latency target is 400 ms to first token.
unknowns: Must the answer ever show these fields?
Is the ticket's owner always the caller?
scenarios.question: How do you limit disclosure?

options.name: Strip or mask personal fields at ingest and enforce ownership in retrieval, with deterministic pattern checks on output
options.why: Data the model never sees cannot be disclosed, and pattern checks add a cheap last line.
options.tradeoff: Some answers lose detail the user could legitimately see.

options.name: Run an LLM judge on every full answer before streaming
options.why: It destroys the first-token target and multiplies cost.
options.tradeoff: Reasonable for rare, high-risk outputs without streaming.

options.name: Scan streamed text in small windows against patterns for sensitive tiers only
options.tradeoff: Patterns miss paraphrases and need tuning.

flips.if: The caller owns the data and sees it anyway
flips.then: Masking adds little. Focus on ownership checks.

flips.if: Answers are batch generated, not streamed

scenarios.takeaway: Prevent at ingest and retrieval, then detect at output.

quiz.q: A client auto-renders the model's Markdown. What is the most serious problem in this output?
options: The image has no alt text
The URL query string carries private data to a third-party host when the client fetches it
quiz.explain: Fetching the image sends the query string to the host, which is the exfiltration. Alt text, Markdown support and length are not the security issue.

quiz.q: Which statements match OWASP LLM07 System Prompt Leakage? Choose all that apply.
options: The system prompt should not be considered a secret
A prompt can be a security control if it is long enough
Sensitive data such as credentials should not be in the prompt
The real risk is delegating authorization to the model
quiz.explain: OWASP says the prompt is not a secret or a control, credentials do not belong there, and the underlying risk is delegated authorization. Length does not make a prompt a control.

flashcards.front: How does Markdown image exfiltration work?
flashcards.back: Injected text makes the model write an image URL whose query string holds private data. The client fetches it automatically and the attacker reads the data from request logs.

flashcards.front: What does OWASP LLM05 advise for model output?
flashcards.back: Treat it as untrusted: encode it for its context, validate before passing downstream, and apply a strict content security policy.

flashcards.front: Is the system prompt a secret or a control?
flashcards.back: Neither, per OWASP LLM07. Keep credentials and authorization logic outside the model, and assume the prompt can be read.
